Messages.Author: Andrew Joubert
Messages.Body:
I have two questions that came up during my last tournament.

1) Is it legal to offer a table split during the seating for the final
round? What about informing a player considering where he is going to sit
about a third player's deck (that intercept deck will eat your 1 stealth
voter alive!)

2) Is it legal to inform a player considering a deal that the player he is
making the deal with broke a deal during a prior round?

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:

> I have two questions that came up during my last tournament.

> 1) Is it legal to offer a table split during the seating for the final
> round?

Sure.

> What about informing a player considering where he is going to sit
> about a third player's deck (that intercept deck will eat your 1 stealth
> voter alive!)

Sure. Also legal to lie about the contents of that deck (or any other).

> 2) Is it legal to inform a player considering a deal that the player he is
> making the deal with broke a deal during a prior round?

Sure. Also legal to lie about deal-breaking history.

>
> Two questions, then:
>
> 1) Is an illegal deal impossible in the finals, since all players can be
> assumed to be playing to win?

A player who is playing to win is, by definition, not in violation of
the "play to win" rule.

If the deal is illegal for some reason, though, like threats or
something, then it is still illegal.

> 2) What about if it isn't the finals? Is a
> table-split-before-the-first-turn then illegal or no or for the losing
> party?

If a player is in violation of any rule, including the "play to win"
aspect of the sportsmanship rule, then that violation is an example of
illegal play, yes.

I'm primarily interested in a confirmation (for what I think is
obvious).

Assuming there is a solid argument (based on encounter in the previous
rounds, etc.), can such a deal ever be legal?

Off the top of my hat:

"In round #2 I had the same predator and prey as now. My defence does
not work against the offence my predator uses, and my offence is
completely countered by the defence my prey uses (they know this, and
chose their relative positions to me based on this knowledge).
However, I can play my deck in a way that ensures that my predator
cannot oust me (but neither can I apply any sort of forward pressure).
I am willing to trade in my otherwise obviously zero VPs for two, but
I need to know from the beginning."

Now, this is basically bullshit, but it is logical and it can be
valid. My gut reaction as a judge to this speech would be something
along the lines of "play the game and let others play it too", and I
would not allow any sort of deal.

Not that I could actually dictate how anyone plays their decks (and in
this case the player can legally go all-out defence because of the
threat, and the "prey" can legally concede after gaining 3 VPs, as the

Messages.Author: d. hathorn

On Wed, 21 Apr 2004, at 7:39am, Wes wrote:

> My point remains. Ruy Lopez is an opening... ie a strategy. You would be
> more likely to find it mentioned in a book of chess openings.
>
> Making deals is a strategy of V:tES. You would be more likely to find
> it mentioned in a newsletter, or in this forum. There is no need for it
> to be in the rules, but I think you know that already.

Except that unlike chess, tournament V:TES has a very unusual rule:
"Players must not play toward goals that conflict with the goal of the
game as stated in the rulebook."

Clearly, this rule may invalidate some strategies, but it's often not very
clear which ones. There are some examples in the V:EKN rules: "attacking
certain players on the basis of their V:EKN ratings or overall tournament
standing, etc." Nevertheless, people have been asking for clarification
on this rule since its inception; I certainly think there's room for more
explicit clarification and more examples, and I don't think requesting
such elaboration is necessarily trolling.

-davey!

Messages.Author: LSJ

Wouter...@yahoo.com (Wouter Kuyper) wrote in message

> So, do i understand it right that in a tourney final
>
> 1) you can take a loosing deal

The only time the rules even notice a deal is when it comes time for a
player to keep a deal in the face of the play to win rule. If making
and honoring that deal (together as a unit) conform to the play to win
rule, then the rules allow it, even if the pieces individually don't
meet the requirements.

As far as what you promise, the rules have no say. You can say what
you like.

> 2) but you have to break it if you can win by that
> (instead of the honouring your deal that is allowed in previous rounds)

If it is not an example of playing to win, then it is illegal under
the play to win rules.

I guess my problem is (and this is assuming I have interpreted your
comments correctly, LSJ), if at a later point in time it actualy works
out that the 2/3 split is the most the "2" player can hope for, then
the deal could be legally honoured.

up until this point. So much so, that the possibility of the GW is
removed (for the 2VP guy).

Do you see my point?

scrote wrote:
> LSJ <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message news:<4083A791...@white-wolf.com>...

>>It's the finals. Since there are no further considerations, players can be
>>assumed to be playing to win.
>
> Are you saying LSJ, that a judge assumes the player taking 2VP's does
> not intend to honour the deal?

I assume you mean in something other than the finals. (Since, as you
quote, players are assumed to be playing to win in the abence of
other, independently-illegal, activity.)

No. The judge needn't do anything at that point.
When it comes time for a player to sacrifice a "playing to win" play
in favor or honoring the deal, then tit must be determined if doing
so doesn't violate the PTW rule (that is, the the deal at the time
it was made was PTW under the assumption that it would be honored).

> Do I have it right? Of course a judge then is required to make sure
> that the player does not honour the deal.

No. The judge is merely required to make sure that the player plays
to win. It could happen that circumstances change such that honoring
the suspect (non-PTW) deal is an example of playing to win at the
time it comes time to honor it.

LSJ expounded:

> Why would a player take a losing deal when he can win?
>
> If the answer involves something illegal (threats, collusion, etc.)
> then that illegal aspect is still illegal.

Guaranteed second place is (in many ways) better than 20% chance of
winning + 20% chance of second etc.
(average prize is certainly higher for instance and if you went into the
table 5th, it looks better still)

In the qualifying rounds you are not allowed to give this consideration
any weight at all -you have to try to win the table. It is
incomprehensible to us that you are apparently saying the opposite for
the final table.
